{{RunningHeader|thank|6265|Thargelia}}'''II.'''† ''intrans.'' To give thanks. {{smaller block|Which we toke as deuoutly as we coude, and ''thanke'' accordyng.{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 39.}}}} '''thanker''' (thang′kėr), ''n.'' [< ''thank'' + ''-er''1.] One who gives thanks; a giver of thanks. {{smaller block|I hope he may long continue to feel all the value of such a reconciliation. He is a very liberal ''thanker.''{{right|''Jane Austen'', Emma, li.}}}} '''thankes'''†, ''n.'' [ME., gen. of ''thank'' used adverbially with the poss. pronouns, meaning 'of his, her, their, my, thy, your, our accord': see ''thank.''] A form used only in the phrases ''his'', ''thy'', etc., ''thankes'', of his, thy, etc., accord; voluntarily. {{smaller block|Ful sooth is seyd that love ne lordshipe Wol noght, ''his thankes'', have no felaweshipe.{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight's Tale, l. 768.}}}} {{smaller block|Thyne herte shal so ravysshed be That nevere thou woldest, ''thi thankis'', lete Ne removen for to see that swete.{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 2463.}}}} '''thankful''' (thangk′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ME. *''thankful'', < AS. ''thancfull'', < ''thanc'', thank: see ''thank'' and ''-ful.''] 1. Impressed with a sense of kindness received, and ready to acknowledge it; grateful. {{smaller block|Be ''thankful'' unto him, and bless his name.{{right|Ps. c. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|As I am a gentleman, I will live to be ''thankful'' to thee for't.{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iv. 2. 89.}}}} {{smaller block|It is no improper Comparison that a ''thankful'' Heart is like a Box of precious Ointment, which keeps the Smell long after the Thing is spent.{{right|''Howell'', Letters, ii. 23.}}}} 2. Expressive of thanks; given or done in token of thanks. {{smaller block|Give the gods a ''thankful'' sacrifice. {{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., i. 2. 167.}}}} {{smaller block|Again and again the old soldier said his ''thankful'' prayers, and blessed his benefactor. ''Thackeray'', Philip, xvii.}} 3†. Deserving thanks; meritorious; acceptable. {{smaller block|Tumaccus thought him selfe happie that he had presented owre men with such ''thankeful'' gyftes and was admitted to theyr frendshippe. {{right|''Peter Martyr'' (tr. in Eden's First Books on America, [ed. Arber, p. 141).}}}} {{smaller block|Thank may you have for such a ''thankful'' part. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney'' (Arber's Eng. Garner, I. 550).}}}} 4†. Pleasing; pleasant. {{smaller block|They of late years have taken this pastime vp among them, many times gratifying their ladies, and often times the princes of the realme, with some such ''thankfull'' noveltie. ''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, ii. (''Davies.'')}} ='''Syn.''' 1. See ''grateful''. ¶ '''thankfully''' (thangk′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''thankfulliche''; < ''thankful'' + ''-ly''2.] In a thankful manner; with grateful acknowledgment of favors or kindness received. {{smaller block|His ring I do accept most ''thankfully''. {{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iv. 2. 9.}}}} '''thankfulness''' (thangk′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being thankful; acknowledgment of a favor received; gratitude. '''thanking†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''thankynge'', < AS. ''thancung'', < ''thancian'', thank: see ''thank'', ''v.''] An expression of thanks. {{smaller block|Therto yeve hem such ''thankynges''. {{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 6041.}}}} {{smaller block|Thanne he wente prevylly, alle be nyghte, tille he cam to his folk, that weren fulle glad of his comynge, and maden grete ''thankynges'' to God Inmortalle. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 227.}}}} '''thankless''' (thangk′les), ''a.'' [< ''thank'' + ''-less.''] 1. Unthankful; ungrateful; not acknowledging kindness or benefits. {{smaller block|That she may feel
How sharper than a serpent's tooth it is
To have a ''thankless'' child! {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 4. 311.}}}} 2. Not deserving thanks, or not likely to be rewarded with thanks: as, a ''thankless'' task. {{smaller block|But whereunto these ''thankless'' tales in vain
Do I rehearse? {{right|''Surrey'', Æneid, ii. 125.}}}} {{smaller block|The Sun but ''thankless'' shines that shews not thee.{{right|''Congreve'', Tears of Amaryllis.}}}} {{smaller|=Syn. See ''grateful.''}} '''thanklessly''' (thangk′les-li), ''adv.'' In a thankless manner; without thanks; ungratefully; in a grudging spirit. {{smaller block|The will of God may be done ''thanklessly.''{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Jehu with Jehoram and Jezebel.}}}} '''thanklessness''' (thangk′les-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being thankless; ingratitude. {{smaller block|Not to have written then seems little less
Than worst of civil vices, ''thanklessness.''{{right|''Donne'', To the Countess of Bedford.}}}} {{smaller|=Syn. See ''grateful.''}} '''thankly†''' (thangk′li), ''adv.'' [< ''thank'' + ''-ly''2.] Thankfully. [Rare.] {{smaller block|He giueth frankly what we ''thankly'' spend.{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas's Weeks, i. 3.}}}} '''thank-offering''' (thangk′of″ėr-ing), ''n.'' An offering made in ancient Jewish rites as an expression of gratitude to God; a peace-offering. {{smaller block|A thousand ''thank-offerings'' are due to that Providence which has delivered our nation from these absurd iniquities. {{right|''Watts.''}}}} '''thanksgive†''' (thangks-giv′), ''v. t.'' [A back-formation, < ''thanksgiving.''] To offer in token of thankfulness. {{smaller block|To ''thanksgive'' or blesse a thing in a way to a sacred use he took to be an offering of it to God. {{right|''J. Mede,'' Diatribe, p. 55. (''Latham.'')}}}} '''thanksgiver''' (thangks-giv′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''thanks,'' pl. of ''thank,'' + ''giver.''] One who gives thanks, or acknowledges a benefit, a kindness, or a mercy. {{smaller block|Wherefore we find (our never-to-be-forgotten) example, the devout ''thanksgiver,'' David, continually declaring the great price he set upon the divine favours. {{right|''Barrow,'' Works, I. viii.}}}} '''thanksgiving''' (thangks-giv′ing), ''n.'' [< ''thanks,'' pl. of ''thank,'' + ''giving.''] 1. The act of rendering thanks or of expressing gratitude for favors, benefits, or mercies; an acknowledgment of benefits received: used in the Old Testament for acknowledgment by the act of offering. {{smaller block|If he offer it for a ''thanksgiving,'' then he shall offer with the sacrifice of ''thanksgiving'' unleavened cakes. {{right|Lev. vii. 12.}}}} {{smaller block|Every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with ''thanksgiving.'' {{right|1 Tim. iv. 4.}}}} '''2.''' A public celebration of divine goodness; specifically [''cap.''], in the United States, Thanksgiving day (see the phrase below). {{smaller block|Great as the preparations were for the dinner, everything was so contrived that not a soul in the house should be kept from the morning service of ''Thanksgiving'' in the church, and from listening to the ''Thanksgiving'' sermon, in which the minister was expected to express his views freely concerning the politics of the country, and the state of things in society generally, in a somewhat more secular vein of thought than was deemed exactly appropriate to the Lord's day.{{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 346.}}}} '''3.''' A form of words expressive of thanks to God; a grace. {{smaller block|There 's not a soldier of us all that, in the ''thanksgiving'' before meat, do relish the petition well that prays for peace.{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 2. 15.}} '''General Thanksgiving,''' in the Book of Common Prayer, a form of thanksgiving, preceding the last two prayers of morning or evening prayer or of the litany, for the general or ordinary blessings of life: so called as distinguished from the forms provided for special persons and occasions.—'''Thanksgiving day,''' a day set apart for a public celebration of divine goodness; specifically, in the United States, an annual festival appointed by proclamation, and held usually on the last Thursday of November. It is celebrated with religious services and social festivities. The first celebration was held by the Plymouth Colony in 1621, and the usage soon became general in New England. After the revolution the custom gradually extended to the Middle States, and later to the West, and more slowly to the South. Since 1863 its observance has been annually recommended by the President.—'''The Great Thanksgiving,''' in early and Oriental liturgies, a form ascribing praise to God for the creation of the world and his dealings with man, now represented by the preface and part of the canon. See ''preface'', 2.}} '''thanksworthy†''' (thangks′wėr″ᴛ̵ʜi), ''a.'' Same as ''thankworthy''. {{smaller block|This seemeth to us in our case much ''thanksworthy.'' {{right|''Bp. Ridley'', in Bradford's Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 168.}}}} '''thankworthiness''' (thangk′wėr″ᴛ̵ʜi-nes), ''n.'' The state of being worthy of thanks. '''thankworthy''' (thangk′wėr″ᴛ̵ʜi), ''a.'' [=G. ''dankwürdig''; as ''thank'' + ''worthy''.] Worthy of or deserving thanks; entitled to grateful acknowledgment. {{smaller block|Nowe wherein we want desert were a ''thankeworthy'' labour to expresse; but, if I knew, I should haue mended my selfe. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie.}} For this is ''thankworthy'', if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully. {{right|1 Pet. ii. 19.}}}} '''thank-you-ma'am''' (thangk′ū-mäm), ''n.'' [Also ''thank-you-mam;'' so called in humorous allusion to the sudden bobbing of the head (as if making a bow of acknowledgment) caused by the jolting when a vehicle passes over the ridge.] A low ridge of earth formed across a road on the face of a hill to throw to one side downflowing rain-water, and thus to prevent the wasting of the road. {{smaller|It also serves to check downward movement of a vehicle and afford relief to the horses both in going up and in going down the hill. Also called ''water-bar.'' [Colloq., U. S.]}} {{smaller block|We jogged along very comfortable and very happy, down steep hills crossed by abrupt and jerky ''thank-you-mams.'' {{right|''Scribner's Mag.'', VIII. 565.}}}} '''thannah''' (than′ä), ''n.'' Same as ''tana''1. '''thanne†''', ''adv.'' A Middle English form of ''than'' and ''then.'' '''Thapsia''' (thap′si-ä̤), ''n.'' [NL. (Tournefort, 1700), < L. ''thapsia'', < Gr. θαψία, θάψος, a plant used to dye yellow, said to have been ''T. Garganica'', brought from the island or peninsula of Thapsus, Sicily; < Θάψος, L. ''Thapsus'', Thapsus.] 1. A genus of umbelliferous plants, of the tribe ''Laserpitieæ.'' {{smaller|It is characterized by a fruit with lateral secondary ridges dilated into broad wings,}} the other ridges filiform, and the seed flat. There are 4 species, natives of the Mediterranean region, especially to the west, and extending to the island of Madeira, where 2 species have a hard and often tall and conspicuous shrubby caudex. They are perennials, or perhaps sometimes bien{{smaller|nials, bearing pinnately decompound leaves with pinnatifid segments, and yellowish, whitish, or purplish flowers in compound umbels of many rays, usually without involucre and with the involucels small or wanting. For ''T. Garganica'', see ''deadly carrot'' (under ''carrot''), also ''asadulcis'', ''laser''1, ''resin of thapsia'' and ''bon-nafa resin'' (under ''resin''). For ''T. decipiens'', a remarkably palm-like species, see ''black parsley'', under ''parsley''. For ''T.'' (''Monizia'') ''edulis'', see ''carrot-tree''.}} [[File:century v08 p0069 c3f1.png|center|325px]] {{c|1, the upper part of the stem with the umbel of ''Thapsia Garganica''; 2, a leaf; ''a'', the fruit.}} '''2.''' [''l. c.''] A plant of this genus. {{smaller block|This ''thapsia'', this wermoote, and elebre,
Cucumber wild, and every bitter kynde
Of herbe is nought for hem. {{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 38.}}}} '''Thapsia plaster.''' {{smaller|See ''plaster''.}} '''thar'''1 (ᴛ̵ʜär), ''adv.'' An obsolete or dialectal form of ''there''. '''thar'''2†, ''v.'' See ''tharf''1. '''thar'''3 (thär), ''n.'' [Also ''thaar'' and ''tahr''; E. Ind.] A wild goat of the Himalayas, ''Capra jemlaica'', also called ''imo'' and ''serow''. {{smaller|The small horns curve directly backward, and the male has a mane of long hair on the neck and shoulders.}} '''tharborough'''† (thär′bur-ō), ''n.'' A corruption of ''third-borough''. {{smaller block|I myself reprehend his own person, for I am his grace's ''tharborough''. {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., i. 1. 185.}}}} '''tharcake''' (thär′kāk), ''n.'' [Also ''thardcake''; for *''tharfcake'', < ''tharf''2 + ''cake''1.] A cake made from meal, treacle, and butter, eaten on the night of the 5th of November. [Prov. Eng.] '''tharf1†''', ''v. t.'' and ''i.'' [Also ''darf;'' < ME. ''tharf'' (often ''thar'', ''dar'', by confusion with forms of ''dare''), inf. ''thurfen'', < AS. ''thearf'', inf. ''thurfan'' = OFries. ''thurf'', inf. ''thurva'' = OHG. ''durfan'' = Icel. ''thurfa'' = Sw. ''tarfva'' = Goth. ''thaurban'', have need, = D. ''durven'' = G. ''dürfen'', dare: see ''dare''1.] To need; lack. {{smaller block|Whanne these tyding were told to themperour of rome he was gretly a-greued, no gome ''thort'' him blame. {{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1076.}}}} {{smaller block|Trwe mon trwe restore, Thenne ''thar'' mon drede no wathe. {{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2354.}}}} {{smaller block|Nece, I pose that he were, Thow ''thruste'' [pret.] nevere han the more fere. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 572.}}}} '''tharf2†''', ''a.'' [< ME. ''therf'', < AS. ''theorf'' = OFries. ''therve'' = MD. ''derf'' = OHG. ''derb'', MHG. ''derp'' = Icel. ''thjarfr'', unleavened.] Unleavened. ''Wyclif.'' {{smaller block|Also thei make here Sacrement of the Awteer of ''Therf'' Bred. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 18.}}}} '''Thargelia''' (thär-gē′li-ä̤), ''n. pl.'' [< Gr. Θαργήλια (sc. ἱερά), a festival of Apollo and Artemis (see def.), < θάργηλος, equiv. to θαλύσιος, in neut. pl. θαλύσια, offerings of first-fruits made to Artemis.] In ''Gr. antiq.'', a festival celebrated at Athens on the 6th and 7th of the month Thargelion, in honor of Delian Apollo and of Artemis. {{smaller block|On the first day of the festival (probably not every year) there was an expiatory sacrifice of two persons, for the men and the women of the state respectively, the victims being condemned criminals; on the second day there were a procession and a contest for a tripod between cyclic choruses provided by choragi.}} {{smaller block|Cases of adoption were very frequent among the Greeks and Romans. . . . In the interest of the next of kin, whose rights were affected by a case of adoption, it was provided that the registration should be attended with certain formalities, and that it should take place at a fixed time—the festival of the ''Thargelia.'' {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', I. 163.}}}}
